programme: TP53 and ZNF148 form the core of a p53-centred DNA-damage/senescence checkpoint (ZNF148's own target list includes TP53, CDKN1A, CDKN2A, ATM and BAK1 — the same apoptosis/cell-cycle-arrest genes TP53 itself regulates via CDKN1A, CDKN2A, GADD45A, MDM2, BAX), with ETV4 acting downstream as the ETS-family effector that converts this checkpoint into either matrix-remodeling/invasion (via MMP1/2/7/13/14, PLAU, PLAUR, CXCL8) or, per one retrieved study, BACE1 transcription following loss of the DNA-damage regulator Ataxin-1.
role_in_a: In Alzheimer's, this axis is expected to govern whether stressed neurons/glia senesce or die versus persist and drive secondary damage: TP53 is flagged as a multi-target hub in an AD systems-biology model, ZNF148 is directly tied to cellular-senescence gene expression in AD, and ETV4 is implicated (via the Ataxin-1 paper) in elevating BACE1 transcription, linking the checkpoint to amyloidogenic processing.
role_in_b: In lung cancer, the same TP53-ZNF148 checkpoint is the genome-stability/apoptosis barrier that tumors mutate, silence, or bypass (TP53 co-mutation status affects EGFR-targeted therapy outcomes; TP53 transcription is epigenetically repressed for cancer-cell persistence), while ETV4 is the downstream effector driving MMP/PLAU-mediated invasion, NSCLC tumorigenesis via MAPK7, and resistance that is targeted alongside EGFR-TKIs.
shared_axis: Both tissues depend on the same TP53–ZNF148 checkpoint to decide a damaged cell's fate, with ETV4 translating that decision into tissue-specific output — invasive remodeling in lung epithelium versus secretase-driving stress response in neurons — so the two diseases would share this module as opposite failure modes (checkpoint bypass enabling proliferation in cancer; checkpoint over-activation contributing to senescence/amyloidogenic stress in brain) of one damage-response network.
reasoning: TP53 and ZNF148 are each independently documented in both diseases (network-hub and senescence-gene studies for AD; mutation/therapy and epithelial-heterogeneity studies for lung cancer), and ETV4's placement in AD rests on a single paper (Ataxin-1/BACE1) that does not name ETV4 in its title, so the module is real but the cross-disease bridge is inferred rather than stated by any source. Cellular senescence is separately an established contributor to both neurodegeneration and cancer biology, which is why 'supported' rather than 'unexpected' fits, but no retrieved paper ties AD and lung cancer together through this exact factor set.
support: 42353021 places TP53 as a systems-biology hub in AD (non-experimental, network pharmacology); 40470298 ties ZNF148 to cellular-senescence gene regulation in AD; 31442405 is the paper through which ETV4 is placed in AD, showing Ataxin-1 loss elevates cerebral BACE1 transcription; 42660014, 42676040, 42495799, 42480692 place TP53 in lung cancer via co-mutation outcomes, epigenetic repression, and MDM2-p53 apoptosis; 42409251, 42100492, 41816486 place ETV4 in NSCLC via autophagy/therapy resistance, USP7-mediated deubiquitination, and combination with EGFR-TKI; 41818350 and 37969391 place ZNF148 in lung cancer via ALK-mutant epithelial heterogeneity and p16/CDKN2A regulation (a shared ZNF148 target).
how_to_falsify: Delete ETV4 in an Ataxin-1-deficient neuronal model and measure BACE1 transcription and amyloid-beta output — if BACE1 induction is unchanged, the AD-side link of the ETV4 arm is wrong. Separately, ChIP for ZNF148 occupancy at the TP53 promoter in senescent lung epithelial cells versus senescent cortical neurons/astrocytes — absence of binding in either tissue would break the claimed shared checkpoint.
caveats: Cross-tissue pairing (brain vs. lung) drawn from 224 patient-group comparisons across only 3 independent cohort pairs, so apparent robustness is partly a count of correlated subgroups rather than independent replications. TP53 is by far the most consistent factor (168/224); ZNF148 and ETV4 are weaker (112–116/224), so the checkpoint core is solid but the invasion/BACE1 effector arm is less consistently recovered. SOX10 was removed as tissue-generic despite topping recurrence (0.72), so this account deliberately avoids leaning on a generic glial/neuroendocrine identity factor; the single-view exclusions (RCOR2, TFDP3, HDAC3, MYCL, etc.) show no chromatin-remodeling complex drove the signal from one cohort alone, supporting that TP53/ZNF148/ETV4 recur across groups rather than being an artifact.
